opus-5.5.text:
I think it's been a pretty dramatic shift, and honestly a bit of a sad one for me personally.

When I was at FAIR, openness was almost part of the identity. You published, you released code, you released models, and the assumption was that science moves faster when everyone can build on each other's work. A lot of the progress in computer vision and representation learning came out of that culture: ResNet, Mask R-CNN, all the self-supervised learning work. People could reproduce things, argue about them, and improve them, and that loop was really healthy.

Over the past few years, especially after large language models showed they could be real products, the incentives changed. Once a model is directly tied to revenue and competitive advantage, the default flips from "why wouldn't we publish this?" to "why would we?" Many labs that used to be very open now share much less. Papers get thinner, technical reports leave out the important details, and sometimes there's nothing at all. I understand the reasons. There's commercial pressure, and there are legitimate safety arguments in some cases. But I don't think we should pretend there's no cost.

The cost is that research becomes less cumulative. If only a few groups know what actually works at scale, the rest of the community, especially academia, ends up either guessing or chasing benchmarks without understanding why things work. Students lose the ability to learn from the frontier. And the field gets more homogeneous, because everyone just tries to replicate whatever the leading closed system seems to be doing instead of exploring different directions.

At the same time, I don't think the story is entirely pessimistic. Open-weight models from several companies, including many strong ones from China, have kept the ecosystem alive and pushed others to respond. And I think academia has an opportunity here. Exactly because the big labs are less open, there's more value in doing work that is transparent, that asks fundamental questions, and that doesn't just depend on having the most GPUs. That's part of why I came back to a university. I still believe that, in the long run, openness wins. Ideas want to spread, and the people who share tend to attract the best collaborators and the best students.

So my view is that the pendulum has swung toward closedness, maybe too far, but it's not a permanent state. It's something we as a community can push back on, by continuing to publish openly, release code and models, and show that open science still produces breakthroughs.

r001.rationale: The response describes reduced publication, thinner papers, incomplete technical reports, and sometimes no disclosure. It does not say labs shifted from research papers to allowing only blog posts.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a pretty big shift, honestly, and I've been on both sides of it. When I was at FAIR, the culture was really that you publish everything. You write the paper, you release the code, you release the weights, and you let the community pick it apart. That was just the default. Nobody questioned it. And a lot of the things people still use today came out of that era, not just from Meta but from Google Brain, DeepMind, everyone was putting stuff out.

What changed, I think, is that once it became clear that scale was the thing, and that the frontier models had real commercial value, the calculus flipped. The recipe itself became the moat. So you see labs that used to publish detailed technical reports now releasing something closer to a marketing document. Model cards with no architecture details, no data details, sometimes not even the parameter count. And I don't want to be too cynical about it, because I understand the pressures. If you spent a hundred million dollars on a training run, your leadership is going to ask why you're giving away the recipe.

But as a researcher, and now as someone back in academia at NYU, I think it's a real loss. Science works by people building on each other's results, and it's hard to build on something when you can't see inside it. I actually think it's created this weird situation where a lot of the important knowledge about how these systems work is tribal now. It moves with people between companies, it doesn't move through papers.

The counterweight has been open weights, which is interesting. Llama, and more recently a lot of the Chinese labs, DeepSeek, Qwen, they've been very open, and that's shifted things back a bit. It's forced the conversation. And on the academic side, I think our job has changed too. We can't compete on scale, so the question is what kind of research still matters when you can't train the biggest model. My answer is that there's actually a lot, especially on the representation side, on understanding what these models actually learn, on the architecture and data questions that industry labs don't have time to study carefully. But we do need to be honest that the center of gravity has moved, and the openness we used to take for granted is something we now have to argue for.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from detailed technical reports toward marketing-style documents and sparse model cards, but does not say labs now permit only blog posts as public research communication.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s been a pretty clear shift toward less openness, especially around the most capable models. And openness isn’t just whether you publish a paper. It’s whether you share enough—the methods, the code, the training details—for somebody outside the lab to understand what happened and build on it.

There’s a tension here. Industry labs are investing a lot, and they have commercial incentives to keep things private. But they also benefit from a research community built on sharing ideas. If that exchange becomes mostly one-way, where companies absorb public research but share less of their own, that’s a problem for the health of the field.

I wouldn’t say every lab is moving in the same direction. There are still meaningful efforts to release models and research. But I think we should look at what those releases actually enable. Can a university researcher study the system, test a claim, or improve it? That’s a more useful measure of openness than the label itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general shift toward less openness, but does not say labs have moved from research papers to allowing only blog posts for public research communication.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s been a pretty clear shift. A few years ago, industry labs were much more willing to publish their research and share details. You could read a paper, understand the approach, and build on it. As AI has become more commercially important, the incentive to share has changed. The research is increasingly tied to the product, so companies are more cautious about what they release.

I understand that from a business perspective, but I worry about what it means for research. Publishing a result without enough detail to reproduce it makes it harder for the community to learn from it or evaluate it. And that especially affects students and academic researchers who don’t have access to the same resources.

I also wouldn’t describe openness as a simple yes-or-no question. Sharing a paper, sharing code, sharing model weights, and sharing training data are different things. A lab can be open in one respect and closed in another. For me, the important question is whether what you share actually enables other people to understand and build on the work.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward greater caution and less detail, but does not say labs moved from publishing research papers to permitting only blog posts.
